A son and his father held a joint fixed deposit with a bank. The son complained that the bank credited the proceeds to the father's account alone. The State Commission refused to hear the complaint, saying it was really a family dispute for the civil court, and the National Commission agreed.

Can a consumer forum refuse to hear a complaint against a bank because the facts also involve a dispute between the joint account holders?

No. A person who avails of a service from a bank is a consumer and can use the consumer remedies. The complaint was against the bank for deficiency in service, not against the father. The State Commission had to decide on the merits whether there was a deficiency in the bank's service. It could not send the complainant to the civil court.

Banks and deposit-taking NBFCs cannot avoid a consumer complaint by pointing to a quarrel between joint holders. They need to be able to show that a payout or premature closure followed the mandate and the terms of the deposit.

Must the NCLT admit a lender's insolvency application?

A power generating company defaulted on bank loans. It asked the NCLT to defer the bank's section 7 application because it held an order of the electricity appellate tribunal in its favour worth about Rs 1,730 crore, more than the bank's claim, which was under appeal. The NCLT and NCLAT held that once debt and default are shown, nothing else is relevant.

Is admission of a financial creditor's application under section 7(5)(a) mandatory once a debt and default are shown?

The Court read the word 'may' in section 7(5)(a), in contrast to 'shall' in section 9(5)(a), as giving the NCLT a discretion. It could consider relevant factors such as the overall financial health and viability of the corporate debtor before admitting. In a later order on a review petition the Court said these observations were made on the facts of the case. In M. Suresh Kumar Reddy v. Canara Bank (2023 INSC 521) the Court held that Vidarbha was confined to its facts and that, once default is shown, admission must ordinarily follow.

For applications decided under the amended section 7(5), the borrower can no longer rely on Vidarbha to resist admission on grounds such as pending claims or general viability. The ruling remains relevant to older matters and to understanding why the provision was rewritten.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 7(5), 9(5)
National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi

Homebuyers who did not file claims

In the insolvency of a real estate developer, several homebuyers filed their claims after the resolution plan had been approved by the committee of creditors and was awaiting the NCLT's approval. The resolution professional and the NCLT refused to take the late claims, and it was argued that the claims stood extinguished.

What happens to homebuyers whose payments and allotments are in the developer's own records but who did not file a claim in time?

Until the NCLT approves the plan, the claims are not extinguished. That does not give late claimants a right to have their claims admitted. The resolution professional is not bound to put late claimants in the list of creditors. But the developer's records show every allottee, the amounts paid and the units allotted, and that liability should be reflected in the information memorandum so that the resolution applicant deals with it. Leaving such homebuyers out is inequitable. The resolution professional was directed to give their details to the resolution applicant, who was to prepare an addendum to the plan for the committee and the NCLT to consider.

Lenders on the committee of creditors of a developer, and bidders, should expect the plan to provide for all allottees shown in the books and not only those who filed claims. That affects the amount available for financial creditors. Home loan lenders can point to this ruling where a borrower's allotment appears in the developer's records but no claim was filed.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 5(8)(f), 29, 30, 31; IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016, regs. 12, 13, 36
Supreme Court · 2022 INSC 630

Recovery certificates and decrees are financial debt

Kotak Mahindra Bank had obtained a recovery certificate from the Debts Recovery Tribunal for a loan, so the certificate arose from a financial debt. It then filed a section 7 application relying on the certificate. The appellate tribunal held that a recovery certificate holder was not a financial creditor.

Is a liability under a DRT recovery certificate a financial debt, and does the certificate give a fresh starting point for limitation?

A liability under a recovery certificate is a financial debt, and its holder is a financial creditor who may file under section 7. A recovery certificate gives a fresh cause of action, so a section 7 application filed within three years of the certificate is in time.

Lenders that have won at the DRT can still use the IBC, but should file within three years of the recovery certificate.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 5(7), 5(8), 7; Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993, s. 19(22); Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 137
National Company Law Appellate Tribunal

Exclusive charge holder in liquidation distribution

A bank with an exclusive charge over certain assets of a company in liquidation relinquished its security and asked to be paid the full sale value of those assets.

Is a secured creditor that relinquishes an exclusive charge paid from the value of that asset, or pro rata with other secured creditors?

Pro rata. After relinquishment, all secured creditors share in proportion to their claims under section 53. The tribunal relied on the Supreme Court's ruling in India Resurgence ARC v. Amit Metaliks (2021).

A lender with an exclusive charge that wants to keep the benefit of it should consider realising the security itself under section 52 rather than relinquishing it.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 52, 53
Supreme Court · 2022 INSC 562

Pledge of demat shares

When a lender invokes a pledge of dematerialised shares and is recorded as beneficial owner, has it 'sold' them and must it credit their value against the debt?

The Depositories Act and its regulations add to, and do not displace, the pledge provisions of the Contract Act. Recording the pledgee as beneficial owner on invocation is not a sale; it only enables the pledgee to sell. The pledge is not discharged, and the pledgee need not account for the shares until an actual sale. The notice under section 176 before sale is mandatory and parties cannot contract out of it. The pledgor may redeem under section 177 until the actual sale. A pledgee cannot sell to itself.

A lender invoking a share pledge must still give reasonable notice and sell to a third party, and should credit the borrower only with the actual sale proceeds. Until then the borrower can redeem.

Statutes: Indian Contract Act, 1872, ss. 172, 176, 177; Depositories Act, 1996; SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 1996, reg. 58
Supreme Court · 2022 INSC 545

State money-lending laws do not apply to NBFCs

NBFCs registered with the Reserve Bank were asked by State authorities in Kerala and Gujarat to take money-lending licences and follow the interest caps in the State money lenders Acts. The Kerala High Court held that the State Act applied to them; the Gujarat High Court held that it did not.

Do State money-lending laws apply to NBFCs registered under the RBI Act and regulated by the Reserve Bank?

No. Chapter III-B of the RBI Act is a complete code, and the Reserve Bank's control over an NBFC runs 'from the cradle to the grave': registration, capital, deposits, prudential norms, directions and winding up. The Kerala Money Lenders Act, 1958 and the Gujarat Money Lenders Act, 2011 have no application to NBFCs registered under the RBI Act and regulated by the Reserve Bank. The Reserve Bank has power to deal with the interest NBFCs charge, through sections 45JA and 45L of the RBI Act.

A registered NBFC does not need a State money-lending licence and is not bound by State caps on interest. Its pricing is governed by the Reserve Bank's directions on interest rates, fair practices and, for microfinance loans, the pricing framework. The ruling does not cover unregistered lenders, and it does not exempt NBFCs from other State laws such as those on coercive recovery, which need to be checked separately.

Statutes: Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, Chapter III-B, ss. 45-IA, 45JA, 45L, 45Q; Kerala Money Lenders Act, 1958; Gujarat Money Lenders Act, 2011
Tripura High Court

Decree holders are not financial creditors

A decree holder filed a public interest petition arguing that the IBC was discriminatory because decree holders were not given a place on the committee of creditors alongside financial creditors.

Must the IBC treat decree holders on a par with financial creditors?

No. Decree holders form a different class from financial creditors, and the classification is reasonable. They have no right to a seat on the committee of creditors. The petition was dismissed.

A decree does not by itself make the holder a financial creditor. A lender's decree or recovery certificate for a financial debt is different: see Kotak Mahindra Bank v. A. Balakrishnan (2022).

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 3(10), 5(7), 21; Constitution of India, Art. 14
Supreme Court · 2022 INSC 217

Business borrowers are not 'consumers'

A stockbroker took an overdraft facility from a bank against a pledge of shares to run his broking business. After a dispute over the sale of pledged shares and the settlement of the account, he filed a consumer complaint claiming deficiency in service.

Is a person who takes a bank facility for his business a 'consumer' who can file a consumer complaint?

No. A service availed for a commercial purpose is outside the definition of 'consumer'. The test is the dominant purpose of the transaction: whether it is closely linked to profit generation. The overdraft was taken to expand the broker's business, so the relationship was purely business to business. The exception for self-employed persons earning a livelihood did not apply.

Lenders facing consumer complaints from business borrowers on working capital, overdraft or trade facilities can raise this as a threshold objection. Individuals borrowing for personal needs, or to earn a livelihood by self-employment, remain consumers.

Statutes: Consumer Protection Act, 1986, s. 2(1)(d) (now Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(7))
Supreme Court · 2022 INSC 156

Liability for fraud by an employee

A couple handed Kisan Vikas Patras with a face value of Rs 32.60 lakh to a post office agent to move them to another post office. The certificates were instead encashed, and Rs 25.54 lakh was paid out in cash through the agent with the involvement of a post office employee. The consumer fora refused relief, treating the agent as the investors' own agent.

Is a post office or bank liable for the fraud or wrongful act of its employee?

Yes. An employer is liable for the fraud or wrong of its employee committed in the course of employment. Proof of the employee's guilt in a criminal case is not required. Payment in cash to someone other than the holder, contrary to the rules, was not a valid discharge under the Negotiable Instruments Act. The post office could not claim to be a holder or payer in due course. The post office and its officers were held jointly and severally liable to pay the maturity value with interest, with Rs 1 lakh as compensation.

Banks, NBFCs and other deposit-takers bear the loss when staff collude in paying out a customer's instrument or deposit to the wrong person. The Court expressly applied the same principle to banks. Controls over cash payouts, identification of the payee and supervision of agents are the practical defence.

Statutes: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, ss. 8, 9, 10, 78, 82; Consumer Protection Act, 1986
Supreme Court · 2022 INSC 44

No writ petition against a private lender's SARFAESI action

An asset reconstruction company that had acquired a loan gave notice of its intention to take possession of the mortgaged properties under the SARFAESI Act. The borrowers filed writ petitions in the High Court, which ordered status quo on a small deposit although about Rs 117 crore was due, and the order continued for years.

Can a borrower challenge a private bank's or ARC's SARFAESI measures by writ petition under Article 226?

A writ petition against a private financial institution or ARC over its proposed action under section 13(4) is not maintainable. Lending and recovery by a private lender is a commercial activity and not a public function. The borrower's remedy is an application to the Debts Recovery Tribunal under section 17. Filing writ petitions to stall recovery was described as an abuse of process.

Private banks, NBFCs, HFCs and ARCs can ask for early dismissal of writ petitions against SARFAESI steps. Borrowers have to use the section 17 route.

Statutes: SARFAESI Act, 2002, ss. 13(2), 13(4), 17; Constitution of India, Art. 226
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 853

Changed terms on renewal

Can a health insurer rely on a new cap on cover that it introduced at renewal without telling the policyholder?

The policyholders were led to believe they were renewing the same policy, while the insurer had introduced caps on certain surgical procedures. The insurer had a duty to tell them about the new limits. Failing to disclose the changed terms was a deficiency in service. The District Forum's order allowing the claim was restored.

Any change to cover at renewal, particularly limits and sub-limits, must be clearly told to the policyholder before renewal. Otherwise the insurer may be held to the earlier terms.

Statutes: Consumer Protection Act, 1986, s. 2(1)(g); IRDAI (Health Insurance) Regulations, 2016
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 826

Pre-existing conditions disclosed at proposal

Can a health insurer reject a claim by citing a medical condition that the insured disclosed, and that the insurer assessed, before issuing the policy?

The insurer must assess the risks from the health condition disclosed in the proposal form before it issues the policy. Once the policy is issued after that assessment, the insurer cannot reject a claim by citing a disclosed existing condition that led to the risk claimed for.

Underwriting must be done before issue. A health insurer that conducted a medical examination and accepted disclosed conditions cannot later rely on them to repudiate.

Statutes: Consumer Protection Act, 1986; Indian Contract Act, 1872 (utmost good faith)
Supreme Court

Lenders cannot be forced into a majority deal

Most of GTL Infrastructure's lenders agreed to sell their loans to an asset reconstruction company, and the GTL group's domestic lenders signed an inter-creditor agreement under RBI's June 2019 stressed assets framework. Canara Bank did neither and filed for insolvency. The borrowers asked the courts to compel it to follow the majority.

Do RBI's rules on sale of loans to ARCs, or the inter-creditor agreement under the June 2019 framework, oblige a dissenting bank to follow the majority of lenders?

No. Under paragraph 6.4 of RBI's Master Circular on prudential norms (IRAC) of 1 July 2015, on sale of financial assets to ARCs, each bank decides for itself whether to accept an offer; the 75% clause does not oblige a dissenting bank to sell. The June 2019 framework did not stop Canara Bank from starting insolvency, and banks cannot be compelled to accept a borrower's settlement or resolution plan. The Bombay High Court's dismissal of the writ petitions was upheld.

Borrowers cannot use RBI's stressed-asset rules to force a lender into a majority deal. The binding effect of the 75% decision is a matter between lenders who signed the inter-creditor agreement.

Calcutta High Court

Stopping invocation of a bank guarantee

A contractor asked the court to restrain the employer from invoking bank guarantees it had furnished, arguing the invocation did not follow the terms of the guarantees.

When can a court stop a beneficiary from invoking an unconditional bank guarantee?

Courts rarely interfere with bank guarantees, but an injunction is available in cases of fraud, irretrievable injustice or special equities, or where the invocation does not conform to the terms of the guarantee. On the facts the invocation was not in terms of the guarantees and special equities existed, so the injunction was confirmed.

Banks paying under guarantees should check that the demand matches the guarantee's terms exactly.

Statutes: Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 126; Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, s. 9
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 704

Lapsed policy revived after the accident

A life policy with an accident benefit rider lapsed in October 2011 for non-payment of premium. The life assured met with an accident on 6 March 2012. The overdue premium was paid on 9 March 2012 without mentioning the accident, and he died later that month. The insurer paid the basic sum assured of Rs 3.75 lakh but refused the additional accident benefit. The consumer fora awarded it.

Is the accident benefit payable when the policy was in a lapsed condition on the date of the accident and was revived afterwards?

No. The policy condition required the policy to be in force when the accident took place. It had lapsed and was revived only after the accident, so the accident benefit was not payable. Paying the overdue premium without disclosing the accident was a suppression of a material fact. Insurance requires utmost good faith from the insured as well. The terms of a policy are to be read strictly. A consumer forum cannot rewrite the contract on grounds of sympathy.

Life insurers can decline rider benefits for an event that occurred while the policy was lapsed, even if the base policy is later revived. Revival processes should ask about events since the lapse.

Statutes: Consumer Protection Act, 1986

Balance sheet entries and limitation

When does limitation run for a lender's insolvency application, and do acknowledgements and recovery decrees restart it?

An application under section 7 or 9 of the IBC is governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act: three years from the date of default. An acknowledgement of a subsisting liability in writing under section 18 of the Limitation Act, which can include an entry in the company's balance sheet, gives a fresh period of limitation. A final decree or a DRT recovery certificate gives the creditor a fresh cause of action to file within three years of it.

Lenders should track acknowledgements (balance sheets, restructuring letters, one-time settlement proposals) to keep claims alive, and can rely on a recovery certificate to start a later insolvency application.

Statutes: Limitation Act, 1963, s. 18, Art. 137; Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, s. 7
Delhi High Court

Pledgor's liability is limited to the pledge

A person pledged securities to a bank for a loan to someone else but was neither the borrower nor a guarantor. After selling the pledged securities, the bank sought to recover the shortfall from him.

Is a third-party pledgor liable for the shortfall after the pledged goods are sold?

No. Under section 176 of the Contract Act, the pawnee can sue the debtor for the shortfall, but a pledgor who is not the debtor or a guarantor is liable only up to the value of the pledged goods.

Lenders who want recourse beyond the pledged assets must take a guarantee from the third-party pledgor.

Statutes: Indian Contract Act, 1872, ss. 172, 176
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 333

Winding up: trustees and SEBI powers

Can trustees wind up a scheme without unitholders' prior consent, and are Regulations 39 to 42 valid?

Regulations 39 to 42 are valid. Being economic regulations, they get judicial restraint. Read together with Regulation 18(15)(c), the trustees' opinion that the scheme should be wound up stands, but the consent of unitholders is a precondition for the winding up.

Trustees cannot close a scheme on their own. They need unitholder consent, which shapes how stress in debt schemes is handled. Under regulation 36(5) of the 2026 Regulations, a scheme reopens for business if consent is not obtained.

Statutes: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, regs. 18(15)(c), 39-42; SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026, regs. 36-38; SEBI Act, 1992
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 297

Personal guarantors after a resolution plan

By a notification of 15 November 2019 the Central Government brought the personal insolvency provisions of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code into force only for personal guarantors to corporate debtors. Promoters and directors who had guaranteed company loans challenged the notification in several High Courts, and the cases were transferred to the Supreme Court.

Could the Government bring Part III of the Code into force only for personal guarantors to corporate debtors, and does approval of the company's resolution plan release the guarantor?

The notification is valid. The Code itself treats personal guarantors to corporate debtors as a separate class, and bringing the provisions into force for that class alone is not excessive delegation. Approval of a resolution plan for the corporate debtor does not by itself discharge the personal guarantor. A discharge of the principal borrower by operation of law, such as in insolvency, does not release the surety. The National Company Law Tribunal dealing with the company's insolvency is also the forum for proceedings against its personal guarantor (section 60(2)).

A lender can pursue the promoter's personal guarantee for the unpaid balance even after the borrower company's resolution plan is approved, and can start insolvency resolution against the guarantor before the NCLT. Whether the guarantee survives still depends on its terms and on the plan: a plan may itself deal with guarantees.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 1(3), 2(e), 31, 60, 95; Indian Contract Act, 1872, ss. 128, 133-135
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 296

Dissenting secured creditor's payout under a plan

An asset reconstruction company held security over the corporate debtor's assets which it valued far above what the resolution plan offered it. The plan was approved by about 95 per cent of the committee of creditors. The ARC voted against it and argued that the committee had to take the value of each creditor's security into account.

Can a dissenting secured financial creditor challenge an approved resolution plan on the ground that it gets less than the value of its security?

No. How the plan money is shared among creditors is a matter for the commercial wisdom of the committee of creditors. A dissenting secured creditor cannot insist on being paid by reference to the value of its security. What the Code assures a dissenting financial creditor is the minimum amount set out in section 30(2)(b). It cannot enforce its security interest outside the plan. Courts review an approved plan only on the limited grounds in sections 30(2) and 61(3).

A secured lender in the minority is bound by the majority's distribution. Its protection is the statutory minimum for dissenting creditors, so its vote and the negotiation inside the committee matter more than a later challenge.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 30(2), 30(4), 31, 53, 61(3)
Delhi High Court · W.P.(C) 3190/2021

Cover for mental illness

Can a health insurer treat mental illness differently from physical illness?

Section 21(4) of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 requires every insurer to provide medical insurance for treatment of mental illness on the same basis as physical illness. Insurers are bound by the Act regardless of any circular. The insurer was ordered to pay costs because the policyholder had to litigate. IRDAI was asked to ensure that all insurers give effect to section 21(4) from 29 May 2018, when it came into force.

Health policies cannot exclude or sub-limit mental illness in a way that does not apply to physical illness. Claims for mental health treatment must be assessed on the same basis.

Statutes: Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, s. 21(4)
National Company Law Appellate Tribunal

Equal ranking of secured creditors in liquidation

In a liquidation, a lender with a first charge on specific assets argued it should be paid from those assets before lenders with a second or no charge on them.

In liquidation, do secured creditors who give up their security keep their priority over particular assets?

No. Secured creditors who relinquish their security to the liquidation estate all rank equally under section 53(1)(b)(ii), whatever their prior inter se priority.

The Supreme Court stayed this ruling on 29 June 2021, and the question of inter se priority is pending before it. Lenders should keep priority arguments open and consider whether to realise security themselves under section 52.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 52, 53
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 216

IBC application versus arbitration

An investor holding optionally convertible redeemable preference shares in Indus Biotech filed a section 7 application, claiming a default on redemption. Indus Biotech asked the tribunal to refer the dispute to arbitration under section 8 of the Arbitration Act.

When a section 7 application and a request to refer the dispute to arbitration are both pending, which comes first?

The tribunal must first decide whether there is a default under section 7. If it admits the application, the proceedings become proceedings in rem and the dispute is no longer arbitrable. If no default is found and the application is rejected, the parties can go to arbitration. On the facts there was no default, and the Court appointed an arbitral tribunal.

An arbitration clause does not stop a lender from filing under section 7, but the tribunal will look at whether a default is really shown before admitting.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, s. 7; Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, ss. 8, 11
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 203

COVID-19 moratorium and interest

Could courts order a full interest waiver, sector-wise relief or a longer moratorium during the COVID-19 pandemic?

Economic and financial policy of RBI and the Government is open to only limited judicial review. Courts will not order particular relief packages, a full waiver of interest or a longer moratorium. No interest on interest, compound interest or penal interest could be charged for the moratorium period. Any amount already recovered had to be refunded or adjusted in the next instalment.

Lenders had to reverse interest on interest and penal interest for the moratorium period for all borrowers. Courts will usually defer to RBI on the design of relief and restructuring schemes, unless they are arbitrary, mala fide or contrary to law.

Statutes: Disaster Management Act, 2005; RBI COVID-19 Regulatory Package circulars, 2020
Calcutta High Court

IBC moratorium does not stop wilful defaulter action

A bank started proceedings to declare a company's directors and guarantors wilful defaulters while the company was under insolvency. The directors argued that the moratorium under section 14 of the IBC barred the bank from proceeding.

Does the IBC moratorium on the company protect its directors and guarantors from wilful defaulter proceedings?

No. The moratorium protects the corporate debtor and its assets. Wilful defaulter proceedings target the conduct of the persons behind the company and are not a recovery action against it. For this purpose the corporate veil can be lifted to look at the conduct of directors and promoters.

Lenders may run wilful defaulter proceedings against promoters, directors and guarantors while the borrower is in insolvency.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, s. 14; RBI Master Circular on Wilful Defaulters
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 133

Cheque bounce cases and the IBC moratorium

Does the IBC moratorium stop section 138 cheque-dishonour cases against a company in insolvency and its directors?

A section 138/141 proceeding against the corporate debtor is a 'proceeding' covered by the moratorium under section 14(1)(a) of the IBC, so it cannot be started or continued against the company during the moratorium. The moratorium protects only the corporate debtor. Directors and other persons in charge named in section 141 of the NI Act remain liable and can be prosecuted. Under section 14(3)(b), a surety under a guarantee of the corporate debtor's debt gets no benefit of the moratorium.

When a corporate borrower enters insolvency, a lender holding dishonoured cheques can still proceed against its signatory directors, and can enforce guarantees, but not against the company itself during the moratorium.

Statutes: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, ss. 138, 141; Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, s. 14
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 104

Bank's duty of care for lockers

A bank broke open a customer's locker without notice, wrongly believing rent was unpaid, and allotted it to someone else. When the customer came to operate it, only some of the ornaments were returned. The consumer fora awarded modest compensation and left the dispute over the contents to a civil court.

What duty does a bank owe a locker holder, and can it be held liable under consumer law for breaking open a locker without notice?

The bank was directed to pay Rs 5 lakh as compensation and Rs 1 lakh as litigation costs. Whatever the contract says, a bank cannot disclaim all responsibility for lockers. It owes a separate duty of care in running the facility. Statutes: Consumer Protection Act, 1986; Indian Contract Act, 1872 (bailment)
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 87

Winding up: unitholders' consent

When trustees wind up a scheme, what does 'consent of the unitholders' under Regulation 18(15)(c) mean?

Consent means consent of a majority of the unitholders who take part in the poll, not a majority of all unitholders of the scheme. Consent of the majority binds all unitholders, including those who did not agree. The Court accepted the e-voting results for the six schemes.

Statutes: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, regs. 18(15)(c), 39
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 59

A pledgor for another's loan is not a financial debtor

A company had pledged shares it held in another company to secure a loan given to its parent. Phoenix ARC, as assignee of the loan, claimed in the pledgor's insolvency as a financial creditor.

Is a lender who holds a pledge from a company for a loan to a different borrower a financial creditor of the pledgor?

No. The pledgor had no liability to repay the loan. Following Anuj Jain (Jaypee Infratech), security alone does not make the lender a financial creditor; at best it is a secured creditor of the pledgor.

Where a group company provides security, lenders should also take a guarantee or make it a co-borrower so that they rank as financial creditors in its insolvency.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 5(7), 5(8); Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 172
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 51

Collusive loans and related parties in the creditors' committee

In the insolvency of a real estate company, two entities connected with its promoter group claimed to be financial creditors on the basis of inter-corporate deposits and a property development arrangement, and sought seats on the committee of creditors. An asset reconstruction company holding genuine debt objected that the transactions were collusive and that the claimants were related parties who had shed that status before the insolvency began.

Are sham or collusive transactions 'financial debt', and can an entity that stopped being a related party before insolvency sit on the committee of creditors?

A transaction that is sham or collusive is not a financial debt, even if it is dressed up as a loan. The money must have been disbursed against consideration for the time value of money in a real transaction. The definition of 'related party' is wide. The bar in the first proviso to section 21(2) is normally tested at the time the committee is formed, but it also covers a creditor that ceased to be a related party only to get around the bar.

Resolution professionals should look at the substance of inter-corporate deposits and at recent changes in shareholding or directorships of claimants. A lender that takes equity, board seats or other control rights in a borrower should check whether it risks being treated as a related party. The Code has a specific carve-out for regulated financial creditors that become related only through conversion of debt into equity.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 5(7), 5(8), 5(24), 21(2)
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 33

Substituting an ineligible arbitrator

HARSAC, a nodal agency of the Haryana government, appointed the State's Principal Secretary as its nominee arbitrator in a dispute with a contractor. The tribunal's mandate later lapsed under section 29A and the contractor applied for a substitute tribunal.

A pending challenge under section 34 means there is a pre-existing dispute, so the section 9 application cannot be admitted. The IBC is not a tool to recover debts or to pressure a debtor into paying an award it is lawfully contesting.

A creditor with an award that is under challenge should enforce it through execution once the challenge fails, not through the IBC.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 8, 9; Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, ss. 34, 36
Supreme Court · 2018 INSC 241

SARFAESI sale and a borrower's conduct

IFCI took action under SARFAESI against a hotel company in Goa and sold the hotel to ITC. The borrower had repeatedly sought time and promised to pay. The High Court set the sale aside for defects in the SARFAESI procedure, including the response to the borrower's objection under section 13(3A).

Can a borrower who has repeatedly sought time and not paid have a SARFAESI sale set aside on procedural grounds?

The secured creditor was entitled to take possession and sell. On the law as it then stood, the borrower's right to redeem the property ended when the sale was made. A borrower whose conduct was to seek time repeatedly without paying cannot rely on non-compliance with section 13(3A), and is not entitled to discretionary relief under Article 226.

Courts look at the borrower's conduct before granting writ relief against a SARFAESI sale. A sale can still be set aside for failure to follow section 13 and the Security Interest Rules. Since the 2016 amendment to section 13(8), the right to redeem ends on publication of the sale notice (Celir LLP, 2023).

Statutes: SARFAESI Act, 2002, ss. 13(2), 13(3A), 13(4), 13(8); Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002
National Company Law Appellate Tribunal

Who pays the interim resolution professional

The NCLT directed the committee of creditors to bear the interim resolution professional's expenses in proportion to their claims. SBI, a committee member, appealed.

Who must bear the interim resolution professional's fees and expenses?

Under Regulation 33 of the CIRP Regulations, the applicant who filed the petition and proposed the interim resolution professional bears the expenses first. The committee of creditors reimburses the applicant to the extent it ratifies the expenses, which then form part of the insolvency resolution process costs.

A lender that files should budget for the interim professional's fees and seek ratification at the first committee meeting.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, s. 5(13); IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016, reg. 33
Delhi High Court

Exclusion of genetic disorders

A policyholder with a heart condition (hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy) was refused a mediclaim payout under an exclusion for 'genetic disorders' that the insurer had added to the policy at a renewal. The trial court decreed his suit, and the insurer appealed.

Is a blanket exclusion of 'genetic disorders' in a health insurance policy valid?

A broad exclusion of all genetic disorders is too wide, ambiguous and discriminatory. It violates Article 14, and it is contrary to public policy when used to deny claims. The right to avail of health insurance is part of the right to health and healthcare under Article 21. The insurance regulator was asked to look again at exclusion clauses so that claims are not rejected on the basis of genetic disorders. The decree for Rs 5 lakh with interest was upheld.

The regulator afterwards told insurers not to reject claims on the basis of a 'genetic disorder' exclusion and standardised the permitted exclusions. Insurers should follow those regulatory requirements; the High Court's wider constitutional conclusions are stayed. Exclusions added at renewal without clear notice to the policyholder are open to challenge.

Statutes: Constitution of India, Arts. 14, 21; Insurance Act, 1938
Supreme Court · 2018 INSC 119

Synchronised and reversal trades

Can pre-arranged, reversed trades in the futures and options segment be manipulative, even though they are cash-settled?

Yes. Trading is meant to make profit. Where one party consistently loses in pre-planned, rapid reversal trades, the trades are not genuine and amount to an unfair trade practice. The Securities Appellate Tribunal was wrong to hold that such trades in the F&O segment cannot manipulate the market because there is no change of beneficial ownership. SEBI's appeals against the brokers were dismissed. Merely facilitating a trade is not a violation, and SEBI had shown no negligence or connivance by the brokers.

Clients who trade in pre-arranged reversals in derivatives are exposed to action even though the trades are cash-settled. A broker is liable only on proof of its own negligence or connivance, so surveillance alerts and records of client instructions matter.

Statutes: SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations, 2003, regs. 3, 4; SEBI (Stock Brokers) Regulations
Supreme Court · 2017 INSC 975

Pre-existing disputes bar operational creditors

Kirusa, which provided tele-voting services, sent Mobilox a demand notice for unpaid invoices and applied under section 9 of the IBC. Mobilox replied that Kirusa had breached a non-disclosure agreement, so the amounts were disputed.

When does a dispute raised by the debtor defeat an operational creditor's insolvency application?

If the debtor shows a plausible dispute about the debt that existed before the demand notice, the tribunal must reject the section 9 application. The dispute need not already be in a suit or arbitration. The tribunal does not decide who is right. It only separates a real dispute that needs further investigation from one that is spurious, hypothetical or patently feeble.

Suppliers, service providers and other operational creditors cannot use the IBC to recover disputed dues. Financial creditors under section 7 are not subject to this test.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 5(6), 8, 9
Supreme Court · 2017 INSC 963

Front-running

Can front-running by persons who are not intermediaries be punished under the PFUTP Regulations?

Information about trades a large investor is about to place is that investor's confidential information. A person who passes on such information in breach of duty, and a 'tippee' who knows of the breach and trades on it, can both be liable for fraud under Regulations 3 and 4(1) of the PFUTP Regulations. Non-intermediary front-running is covered.

Fund managers, dealers and anyone with advance knowledge of a fund's orders, and those they tip off, are exposed to SEBI action. AMCs need controls on order information and on staff and related-party trading.

Statutes: SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices relating to Securities Market) Regulations, 2003, regs. 3, 4(1); SEBI Act, 1992
Supreme Court · 2017 INSC 837

Admission of a creditor's insolvency petition

ICICI Bank applied under section 7 of the IBC to start insolvency against Innoventive Industries. The company argued that its liabilities stood suspended by a Maharashtra government notification under the Maharashtra Relief Undertakings (Special Provisions) Act, 1958, so no debt was payable.

What must the tribunal examine before admitting a financial creditor's application, and can a State relief law suspending a company's debts block insolvency under the IBC?

On a section 7 application the tribunal only has to be satisfied that a default has occurred, that is, that a financial debt was due and has not been paid. The debtor may show that the debt is not due or not payable in law, but the creditor need not prove more. The Maharashtra Act is repugnant to the IBC, a later Parliamentary law on the same subject, and gives way to it under Article 254 of the Constitution. A State law suspending liabilities cannot stop an IBC process. The IBC is a complete code designed for speed; the tribunal must decide admission within the statutory timelines.

Lenders filing under section 7 need clear proof of the debt and the default (loan documents, statements, record from an information utility). Arguments about the borrower's general hardship or other relief schemes do not defeat admission. Later rulings refined the discretion to admit, but default remains the trigger for a financial creditor's petition.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 3(12), 7, 238; Constitution of India, Art. 254
Insurance Ombudsman, Pune

Early death claim under loan-linked group life cover

A borrower was covered under a group term life policy taken with a loan from an NBFC. She died 362 days into the cover. The insurer rejected the death claim because she had not disclosed treatment for cancer in the proposal, and the cause of death was related to it.

What is payable where a life insurer proves suppression of a material fact but does not allege fraud?

The insurer proved the non-disclosure with cogent evidence, so the rejection of the death claim stood. Because the insurer had not alleged fraud, the amended section 45 of the Insurance Act required it to refund the premium paid. It was directed to do so.

For loan-linked group life cover sold through lenders, the health declaration taken at the time of the loan decides whether an early claim is paid. Lenders acting as master policyholders should make sure borrowers complete it themselves. Where a claim within three years is rejected for misstatement not amounting to fraud, the insurer has to refund the premiums.

Statutes: Insurance Act, 1938, s. 45 (as substituted in 2015); Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017
Supreme Court · 2017 INSC 593

Enforcing an arbitral tribunal's interim orders

A party ignored interim orders made by an arbitral tribunal under section 17 of the Arbitration Act. The tribunal referred the default to the court under section 27(5), but the Bombay High Court held that it had no power to punish for such disobedience.

Can disobedience of an arbitral tribunal's interim order be punished as contempt?

Yes. Under section 27(5), a person who fails to comply with an arbitral tribunal's interim order is guilty of contempt of the tribunal, and the tribunal may make a representation to the court, which can punish as for contempt of court. From 23 October 2015 section 17(2) also makes the tribunal's interim orders enforceable as if they were orders of the court.

Lenders that get interim relief from an arbitral tribunal (for example, to secure a vehicle or deposit funds) can enforce it through the court.

Statutes: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, ss. 17, 27(5)
Insurance Ombudsman, Ahmedabad

24-hour hospitalisation and day-care procedures

An insured under a family floater policy had two intravitreal injection procedures for a retinal condition, costing Rs 50,225 in all. The insurer refused both claims, saying the hospital stay was under 24 hours, the treatment could have been taken as an out-patient and it was 'unproven'.

Can a claim be refused for a stay of less than 24 hours where the procedure is done in an operation theatre by a specialist?

No. Procedures that once needed longer admission are now done in a few hours because of advances in technology. Eye surgery was covered by the policy's day-care clause with no 24-hour condition. The treatment needed an operation theatre and a specialist and was not an ordinary out-patient treatment. The insurer did not prove that it was unproven. The claim was allowed, less the policy's 10 per cent co-payment.

Insurers should test short-stay claims against the day-care clause and the nature of the procedure, and should state one clear ground of rejection. A different award in the same compilation upheld rejection where the procedure was not in that policy's day-care list, so the wording of the policy decides the outcome.

Statutes: Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017
Insurance Ombudsman, Ahmedabad

'Reasonable and customary charges' deductions

A senior citizen claimed Rs 62,227 for cataract surgery. The insurer paid Rs 32,927 and disallowed the rest under the policy's 'reasonable and customary charges' clause, saying a multifocal lens was a betterment she did not need.

What must an insurer show before cutting a health claim as above reasonable and customary charges?

The insurer must prove that the charges were unreasonable, by reference to prevailing charges for the same treatment in the same area. It produced no comparative rates, so the deduction was arbitrary. The surgeon's fee and the actual cost of the lens could not be treated as unreasonable. The insurer was directed to pay a further Rs 23,323.

A 'reasonable and customary' deduction needs evidence: rate comparisons for the same provider type and geography. An insurer's or administrator's opinion on what the patient needed is not enough.

Statutes: Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017
National Company Law Appellate Tribunal

Admission without notice set aside

The NCLT admitted ICICI Bank's section 7 application against Starlog Enterprises ex parte. The company had not been served, and the claim did not match the record.

Can a section 7 application be admitted without notice to the company?

The admission was set aside. The company must be given notice and a hearing before admission, and the claim and default must be properly shown. Costs were imposed on the bank.

Lenders must serve the application and get the figures right; defective filings delay the process and can attract costs.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, s. 7
Insurance Ombudsman, Ahmedabad

Non-disclosure at portability unrelated to the claim

A family had been continuously insured since 2000 and moved to a new general insurer under portability in 2015. A claim of about Rs 2.06 lakh for the wife's knee replacement was rejected because her ten-year history of hypertension had not been mentioned in the proposal form at portability.

Can a ported health policy claim be rejected for non-disclosure of a condition that has no connection with the treatment claimed?

The complaint was allowed and the insurer was directed to pay the claim in full. There was no nexus between hypertension and the knee replacement, and the benefits accrued over fifteen years under the earlier policies were available to the insured after portability.

Health insurers should not reject a claim on a non-disclosure that is unrelated to the illness treated, least of all on a ported policy that carries continuity benefits.

Statutes: Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017
Calcutta High Court

Hearing the company before admission

A company against which a bank had filed a section 7 application challenged the validity of section 7, arguing it did not give the company a hearing before admission.

Is section 7 valid, and must the tribunal hear the company before admitting a financial creditor's application?

Section 7 is valid. The tribunal must follow natural justice, which section 424 of the Companies Act makes it apply, so the company must be given notice and a chance to be heard before admission.

Lenders filing under section 7 must serve the application on the company. Admission without notice can be set aside (see Starlog Enterprises).

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, s. 7; Companies Act, 2013, s. 424
Bombay High Court

Lone lender's winding-up petition while JLF restructures

IDFC Bank, holding about 1% of Ruchi Soya's debt, filed a winding-up petition. The other lenders, holding about 98% of the debt, were working on a revival plan through a joint lenders' forum under RBI's framework.

Should a winding-up petition by a small lender be admitted while the joint lenders' forum is pursuing revival?

The petition was dismissed. Winding up is discretionary, and the court considered the wishes of the overwhelming majority of lenders who were pursuing revival under RBI's framework.

Winding up has since been replaced by the IBC for insolvency, where any financial creditor may file on default. Ruchi Soya itself went through the IBC later.

Statutes: Companies Act, 1956, ss. 433, 434; RBI Framework for Revitalising Distressed Assets, 2014
Supreme Court · 2016 INSC 201

Proof of manipulation by brokers

What proof does SEBI need to hold a broker or sub-broker liable for manipulative trading?

Direct proof of a meeting of minds is rarely available. Civil liability under the SEBI Act and its regulations is decided on the preponderance of probabilities; prosecution needs proof beyond reasonable doubt. Liability can be inferred from circumstances such as the volume of trades, how long trading in a scrip persisted, the details of buy and sell orders and how close in time they were.

Brokers can be penalised on circumstantial evidence for trades placed for clients, especially in illiquid scrips. Know-your-client checks, surveillance alerts and records of client instructions are the broker's main defence.

Statutes: SEBI Act, 1992; SEBI (Stock Brokers and Sub-Brokers) Regulations, 1992; SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations, 2003
Supreme Court · 2015 INSC 946

Assignment of life policies

Could an insurer refuse to register assignments of life policies made for trading?

Under section 38 as it then stood, life policies were transferable and assignable. Once the procedure was followed, the insurer had to register the assignment, and its circular refusing assignments for trading was ultra vires. The Court noted that section 38 as amended by the Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act, 2015 now gives the insurer discretion whether to accept a transfer or assignment.

Today an insurer may decline to act on an assignment where it has sufficient reason to believe the assignment is not bona fide, not in the policyholder's interest or in public interest, or is for trading in policies. It must record its reasons in writing before refusing (section 38(2) and (3)).

Statutes: Insurance Act, 1938, s. 38
Supreme Court · 2015 INSC 942

RBI inspection reports under RTI

Can RBI refuse to disclose inspection reports and other information about the entities it regulates under the Right to Information Act?

RBI does not hold such information in a fiduciary relationship with the banks it regulates, and cannot refuse disclosure on the grounds of economic interest or commercial confidence in this case. Inspection reports and similar documents obtained by RBI from a regulated entity are 'information' under section 2(f) of the RTI Act. RBI's duty is to the public, not to the regulated entity.

Findings in RBI inspection reports can become public through RTI requests, subject to the exemptions in section 8 that apply on the facts. Regulated entities should expect supervisory findings to be disclosable.

Statutes: Right to Information Act, 2005, ss. 2(f), 8(1)
Bombay High Court

NBFC outside a CDR package

An NBFC had given a term loan of about Rs 50 crore to a construction company. When the company defaulted, its banks put it into corporate debt restructuring (CDR), which the NBFC had not joined. The NBFC sought interim relief, a receiver and winding up.

Can an NBFC outside a CDR package wind up the borrower or seize its assets while the banks' restructuring is under way?

The court refused to admit the winding-up petition while the CDR package was in progress. The receiver and the injunction were vacated. The NBFC was allowed to join the CDR, and otherwise had to be told before any disposal of assets.

Under the IBC a lender that has not joined a restructuring can still file on default, and RBI's framework now binds only lenders who sign the inter-creditor agreement.

Statutes: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, s. 9; Companies Act, 1956, ss. 433, 434
Supreme Court · 2014 INSC 678

Exchange's lien over a defaulting broker

When a broker defaults, who gets paid first from the membership card and the deposited securities: the stock exchange or the Income Tax Department?

A membership card is only a personal privilege granted by the exchange under its rules. Its sale proceeds cannot be paid over to the Income Tax Department for the member's tax dues. For securities deposited with the exchange, the exchange's lien makes it a secured creditor with priority over Government dues.

Securities a broker has deposited with the exchange are first applied to the broker's obligations under the exchange's rules, ahead of tax dues. The membership card's value is not available to the tax department.

Statutes: Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and Rules; Income Tax Act, 1961, s. 226(3)
Gujarat High Court

Wilful defaulter rules and independent directors

Two borrowers and their directors challenged RBI's Master Circular on wilful defaulters of 2 July 2012 and show-cause notices issued to them by banks. One petition was against a private sector bank.

Is RBI's wilful defaulter regime valid, and can it be applied to every director of a defaulting company?

The Master Circular is valid, including the bar on fresh credit and the five-year bar on new ventures. It has statutory backing under the Banking Regulation Act. Treating every director as a wilful defaulter regardless of role is arbitrary. Only directors shown to be responsible may be named, and promoter-directors are treated differently. A show-cause notice must give particulars of the alleged wilful default. A private bank is not amenable to the writ jurisdiction, so the petition against it was not maintainable.

Lenders must identify the specific role of each director before naming them. RBI's current wilful defaulter directions build in these safeguards: non-whole-time directors are named only where their involvement is shown.

Statutes: Banking Regulation Act, 1949, ss. 21, 35A; RBI Master Circular on Wilful Defaulters, 2 July 2012; Constitution of India, Arts. 14, 19(1)(g), 226
Delhi High Court

Exclusive charge holder outside CDR

Yes Bank held an exclusive charge over certain assets of a borrower. The borrower went into corporate debt restructuring, which Yes Bank did not join, and the CDR package proposed sharing that security with the other lenders.

Can a lender with an exclusive charge be made to share its security under a restructuring it did not join?

No. A CDR package binds only lenders who are party to it. Yes Bank was entitled to protect its exclusive charge, and the borrower was restrained from dealing with the charged assets.

Lenders that do not sign an inter-creditor agreement are not bound by the majority's decisions, but the resolution plan must give dissenting lenders at least their liquidation value.

Statutes: Indian Contract Act, 1872; Transfer of Property Act, 1882, s. 48; Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX
Supreme Court · 2011 INSC 793

Repossession by force

Can a financier take back a vehicle by force under a hire-purchase agreement?

Even for goods under hire-purchase, recovery must follow the law. The owner-financier cannot use force to take back possession on the strength of the agreement. RBI's guidelines support this. Recovery in breach of those guidelines, or of the principles laid down by the Supreme Court, will be struck down.

Vehicle and asset financiers must repossess through lawful process, with no force or intimidation. Recovery agents act for the lender, and the lender answers for them. Consumer forums can award compensation for unlawful repossession.

Statutes: Consumer Protection Act, 1986; RBI Fair Practices Code and recovery guidelines
Supreme Court · 2011 INSC 739

Title only by registered conveyance

Do sale agreements, general powers of attorney and wills ('GPA sales') transfer title to immovable property?

Immovable property can be transferred only by a registered deed of conveyance. 'SA/GPA/Will' transactions neither convey title nor create any interest in the property, except to the limited extent of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. Such documents cannot be treated as title deeds or used for mutation in municipal or revenue records.

Lenders taking a mortgage must check that the mortgagor's title rests on registered conveyances. A chain built on GPA sales gives no mortgageable title and the security may fail.

Statutes: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, ss. 53A, 54; Registration Act, 1908, ss. 17, 49; Indian Stamp Act, 1899
